identity.title: Capturing the Temporal Dependence of Training Data Influence

problem.claim: How to measure the influence of training data as a function of its position in, and interaction with, the optimization trajectory.

gap.claim: Influence-function methods assume permutation-invariant learning, an assumption violated by stochastic, non-convergent, multi-stage training sensitive to data ordering.

contributions.claim: Formalizes trajectory-specific leave-one-out influence for removing a data point at a particular training iteration while accounting for the encountered data sequence and optimization trajectory.
Introduces data value embedding, which approximates trajectory-specific leave-one-out influence using a training-data embedding and a test-data gradient dot product.
Reports distinct influence phases, with early- and late-stage data points exerting greater impact on the final model, and connects this pattern to timing data selection.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe data value embedding as a novel technique for efficiently approximating trajectory-specific leave-one-out influence.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that data value embedding captures training-data ordering and reveals distinct phases of data influence.
The authors report that early- and late-stage training data have greater impact on the final model, motivating strategically timed data selection to manage selection overhead.

narrative_sequence.summary: Existing influence estimation assumes training-order permutation invariance.
Modern stochastic, multi-stage, non-convergent curricula depend on data ordering, creating unanswered stage-specific and trajectory-dependent influence questions.
The paper defines trajectory-specific leave-one-out influence and proposes data value embedding with dot-product approximation.
The embedding is reported to expose stronger influence in early and late training stages, suggesting timed data selection.

source_observation.claim: The abstract ties a failure of a standard assumption to a trajectory-aware quantity and then to an approximation whose inputs are explicitly identified.

lessons.interpretation: A strong technical narrative can align the limitation, formal target, computational obstacle, and proposed estimator in sequence.
lessons.application: When presenting a new influence or attribution method, state the violated assumption, define the target quantity, identify the cost bottleneck, and show exactly how the estimator approximates it.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when the work does not introduce a formal target or when the main contribution is primarily empirical or architectural.

unknowns: The abstract does not report quantitative approximation error, computational cost, datasets, baselines, or experimental conditions.
It does not specify how influence phases are measured or whether the reported pattern holds across models, curricula, or selection settings.
